# ReasMark: A Robust Watermark for Attributing LLM Reasoning Under Knowledge Distillation Attacks

- **Authors**: Peizhuo Lv, Ruihua Zhou, Yunpeng Li, Ruigang Liang, Xingshuo Han, XiaoFeng Wang, Wei Dong, Yuling Liu
- **Venue**: ACL
- **Published**: unknown
- **Source**: anthology

- **PDF**: <https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.2185.pdf>
- **DOI**: 10.18653/v1/2026.acl-long.2185
- **Topics**: overthinking
- **Relevance score**: overthinking 0.40

## In one line

ReasMark protects proprietary reasoning models' intellectual property by training them to systematically produce longer chains-of-thought for prompts dominated by a secret 'long' high-frequency-token set and shorter chains for a 'short' token set (plus a matching entropy signature), so that a student model distilled from the protected model inherits this reasoning-length watermark and can be detected black-box via a one-sided t-test, surviving knowledge distillation, pruning, quantization and LoRA fine-tuning attacks where standard token-distribution watermarks fail.

## Problem

Reasoning-enhanced LLMs represent substantial proprietary investment (e.g. Grok 4 training estimated at 310 GWh/$490M) and their reasoning behavior is now a distinct target for theft via knowledge distillation -- an adversary can query a deployed reasoning model as a black-box teacher and train a student to replicate its outputs including intermediate reasoning traces -- but existing LLM watermarking methods operate on surface-level token distributions or decoding-time biases, which distillation training (which matches semantic behavior rather than exact token reproduction) attenuates or removes entirely, leaving reasoning behavior itself unprotected.

## Contributions

- the first black-box watermarking approach specifically designed to remain verifiable for LLM reasoning *behavior* (not just surface text) under knowledge-distillation attacks, by embedding the watermark into how the model reasons rather than into decoding-time token biases
- input-domain entanglement, deriving watermark tokens from the target domain's own high-frequency prompt vocabulary so that any realistic distillation query is likely to activate the watermark, without needing artificial trigger phrases
- a score-conditioned dual-loss embedding (reasoning-length control plus entropy regularization) that creates a statistically detectable, distillation-robust reasoning-length gap while preserving main-task accuracy and reasoning faithfulness (measured via Early Answering AOC)
- comprehensive validation across 3 models, 3 domains, cross-dataset and cross-domain generalization, 3 distillation attack types, and 4 post-deployment watermark-removal attacks (pruning, LoRA fine-tuning, quantization), consistently outperforming 5 surface-token watermarking baselines whose detectability collapses to near-random after distillation

## Method

ReasMark has three components. (1) Input-domain entanglement: computes token frequencies over the target-domain's own prompt distribution, retains the top-K high-frequency tokens, and randomly partitions n of them into disjoint 'long' (L) and 'short' (S) watermark token sets -- because these come from the natural high-frequency vocabulary rather than artificial trigger phrases, any prompt an adversary uses for distillation queries will, with high probability, contain watermark tokens, making the watermark essentially unavoidable to activate. Each prompt gets a signed long-short score r(x) in [-1,1] based on its relative count of L vs. S tokens. (2) Behavioral watermark embedding: adds two score-conditioned regularizer losses on top of the standard task loss during fine-tuning -- L_think encourages long-token-dominated prompts (r(x)>0) to lower their probability of emitting the thinking-termination token (producing longer reasoning) and short-token-dominated prompts to raise it (producing shorter reasoning), calibrated relative to a moving-average baseline so the model's overall length distribution is preserved globally while a systematic length gap opens between long- and short-dominated prompts; L_ent additionally pushes long-dominated prompts toward higher token-level predictive entropy and short-dominated prompts toward lower entropy, distributing the watermark signal across the whole trace (not just the termination point) to make it harder for a student to average away. (3) Black-box verification: constructs paired probes (a long-token-enriched and a short-token-enriched variant of the same base prompt), queries the suspect model, measures the resulting reasoning-length difference for each pair, and applies a one-sided one-sample t-test on the mean paired difference across probes to determine whether the suspect model exhibits the same long-short-dependent reasoning-length pattern as the protected model.

## Results

Across three teacher/student model pairs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B-Thinking, Phi-4-mini-reasoning) and three domains (OpenMathReasoning, OpenCodeReasoning, R1-Distill-SFT/general), unwatermarked base models show no statistically significant reasoning-length gap (p>0.05 in all cases), confirming no false-positive detection. After ReasMark fine-tuning, the watermark is statistically significant (p<0.05) in every teacher/domain combination while main-task accuracy stays close to the unwatermarked baseline (e.g. DeepSeek base 0.580 ACC -> watermarked 0.570 on OpenMathReasoning). Critically, students distilled from watermarked teachers consistently and significantly retain the watermark (p<0.05 in every one of 9 tested distillation configurations across teacher/student/domain combinations), e.g. distilling from watermarked DeepSeek to a Qwen student on OpenMathReasoning yields d-bar=468.2, p=0.027, confirming the student inherits the teacher's reasoning behavior pattern rather than merely copying final answers. The watermark generalizes across datasets within the same domain (embedded on OpenMathReasoning, still detected on held-out MATH and GSM8K, p<0.05) and across domains from a single embedding pass on a mixed corpus (OpenThoughts-114k, detected on both math and code test sets). ReasMark remains detectable against diverse distillation attack types: optimization-based (MiniLLM, DistiLLM) and API-based (Alpaca-style) extraction, all p<0.05, with distilled-student accuracy close to the teacher's (>=0.560 vs. 0.570). Compared against five representative surface-token watermarking baselines (KGW, Unigram, SWEET, EXP, SynthID-Text), those methods achieve near-perfect detectability before distillation (AUROC~1.0) but at severe main-task accuracy cost (ACC dropping to 0.270-0.290 vs. 0.580 for the unwatermarked base model), and their detectability collapses to near-random (AUROC~0.5) after distillation because distillation training matches semantic behavior rather than exact surface tokens; ReasMark instead preserves main-task accuracy (0.570 before, 0.585 after distillation) while remaining significantly detectable both before (p=0.005) and after (p=0.020) distillation. An ablation shows L_main alone creates no watermark; L_think alone creates a strong pre-distillation signal (d-bar=631.9) that weakens to non-significance after distillation (p=0.069); L_ent alone is insufficient pre-distillation (p=0.065) but helps the signal survive distillation; only the full combined loss achieves both a strong pre-distillation watermark and a significant post-distillation one (p=0.020). A long/short token-set-size sweep finds n=60 optimal (too few tokens, e.g. n=10, gives an insufficiently stable watermark; too many, e.g. n=80-100, degrades main-task accuracy from limited training data coverage). Reasoning-faithfulness analysis (via the Early Answering AOC metric) shows AOC stays stable across base, watermarked, and distilled models, indicating the watermark modulates reasoning length/entropy without introducing redundant steps or distorting reasoning faithfulness. ReasMark also survives watermark-removal attacks on distilled students (structured attention/FFN pruning at 20%, LoRA instruction fine-tuning, 8-bit/4-bit quantization), remaining significantly detectable (p<0.05) in all cases while student accuracy stays above 0.560, though LoRA fine-tuning weakens the signal most (p=0.045, the closest to the significance threshold among tested attacks).

## Limitations

The watermark's activation depends on target-domain prompts naturally containing enough high-frequency long/short watermark tokens; the paper's own token-set-size ablation shows too few tokens (n<=20) produce an insufficiently stable signal, meaning the approach's robustness is somewhat sensitive to this hyperparameter and to the specific prompt distribution of the protected domain. Verification requires the ability to construct paired long/short probe variants and query the suspect model's reasoning trace directly (assuming reasoning traces are exposed, as in DeepSeek-R1/Qwen3/Gemini-style deployments); the method's applicability to reasoning models that fully hide their intermediate traces from API users is not addressed. Among the tested post-deployment attacks, LoRA instruction fine-tuning weakens the watermark signal the most (p rising to 0.045, closest to the 0.05 threshold), suggesting targeted fine-tuning attacks may pose a comparatively greater risk to the watermark's robustness than pruning or quantization.

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: Tangential in motivation (intellectual-property protection, not efficiency) but directly relevant in mechanism: ReasMark deliberately trains a model to produce systematically longer or shorter reasoning traces for different prompts, using a thinking-termination-token probability loss and an entropy-based regularizer, as a controllable, distillation-robust length-modulation signal. This is technically similar to (though motivated oppositely from) the length-control mechanisms other papers in this archive use to *shorten* overthought traces -- and its explicit check that the induced length/entropy manipulation does not distort reasoning faithfulness (via the Early Answering AOC metric) is a useful methodological reference for evaluating whether a length-control intervention preserves genuine reasoning quality.

## Abstract

Reasoning-enhanced large language models rely on intermediate reasoning signals to solve complex, multi-step tasks, making reasoning behavior a valuable form of intellectual property. Meanwhile, knowledge distillation enables an adversary to replicate this behavior in a realistic black-box setting by repeatedly querying a deployed model on a target domain and training a local student to imitate its outputs, including reasoning traces. Existing LLM watermarks primarily operate on surface text and decoding-time token biases, and thus fail to provide reliable attribution of reasoning behavior once it is transferred through knowledge distillation. ReasMark entangles the watermark with the target-domain input distribution by selecting watermark tokens from high-frequency prompts, so distillation queries naturally activate it. It then embeds the watermark by score-conditioned losses that create a detectable reasoning-length gap for black-box verification. Comprehensive experiments across multiple LLMs, datasets, and distillation settings demonstrate that ReasMark consistently outperforms existing baselines while preserving task utility.
